articles.title: Our New Reseller Never Registered Our Replacement Laptops and Every Depot User Who Switched One On Became Its Administrator
articles.excerpt: Since 2023 a replacement laptop for anyone at a depot has gone straight from our reseller to the depot. The user switches it on, connects to the Wi-Fi, signs in with a work account, and Windows Autopi…
articles.body: Since 2023 a replacement laptop for anyone at a depot has gone straight from our reseller to the depot. The user switches it on, connects to the Wi-Fi, signs in with a work account, and Windows Autopilot does the rest. It joins the laptop to our directory, enrols it in our device management, installs our applications and sets the user up without administrator rights. Nobody from my team touches it, which matters when our nearest engineer can be two hours away. That only works because the laptop is known to us before it is switched on. When we order, the reseller uploads each laptop's hardware hash, a fingerprint of the machine, to our tenant, and Autopilot recognises it the first time it starts. In April 2025 purchasing moved our laptop orders to a cheaper reseller.
articles.author: Serguey Shinder

articles.title: Hackers sat inside 3 AI companies, copying the messages people sent to AI
articles.excerpt: Hackers sat inside three AI companies, copying the messages people sent to AI. None of the three knew until a security firm told them. One password from those messages was used the next day. On 19 Nov…
articles.body: Hackers sat inside three AI companies, copying the messages people sent to AI. None of the three knew until a security firm told them. One password from those messages was used the next day. On 19 Nov 2026, HD Moore, Chief Research Officer at Dragos, published the results of a five-month experiment. From July through November 2026, the team submitted approximately two million prompts to widely used AI services. The prompts carried unique URLs and canary credentials, such as fake AWS keys (passwords to Amazon cloud accounts), that existed nowhere else. If anyone used one of those secrets, someone had read the prompt that carried it. The secrets were used. Here is what the research shows, and what it means for any business whose staff or software send prompts to AI services.

articles.title: From clicking to three lines of script: the shortest path to automation
articles.excerpt: From clicking to three lines of script: the shortest path to automation Automation usually begins not with learning a tool but with writing down the path you keep retyping. Written in the order we act…
articles.body: From clicking to three lines of script: the shortest path to automation Automation usually begins not with learning a tool but with writing down the path you keep retyping. Written in the order we actually hit the problems, so the fixes land in context. Which form when One-off with visual feedback (graphics, media) → GUI. Batch, scheduled, or in CI → CLI. Team must perform it identically → CLI plus a one-page parameter cheat sheet; do not encode procedure in someone's muscle memory. Plenty of workflows want both: explore in the GUI, then freeze the successful path as a script. Three ways to pin a workflow Aliases — collapse an eight-flag invocation to two letters. Config files — anything repeatable belongs on disk, not in recall.

articles.title: Your Mentee Has to Present a Research Paper at the Team's Reading Group
articles.excerpt: Your mentee's team has started a monthly reading group, and it is their turn next. They have picked a well known paper about a distributed database, fourteen pages long, full of diagrams and proofs. T…
articles.body: Your mentee's team has started a monthly reading group, and it is their turn next. They have picked a well known paper about a distributed database, fourteen pages long, full of diagrams and proofs. They have read the first three pages twice and understood very little. The session is in nine days, and they ask you, a bit embarrassed, whether there is a trick to it. There is, and it is worth telling them that almost nobody reads a paper from the first word to the last. In 2007 S. Keshav, a computer science professor, published a short article called How to Read a Paper. He suggests reading in three passes. The first takes five to ten minutes: the title, the abstract and introduction, the section headings, the conclusions, and a glance at the references.

articles.title: From a Fresh Project to a Running API with ZinTrust

articles.body: When starting a new API project, the last thing you want is to spend your first hour dealing with setup. You want to get the project running, understand how things fit together, and start building. That's the idea behind ZinTrust: make the initial setup straightforward so you can get to the actual work sooner. Getting started You can create a new ZinTrust project with a few commands: npm install -g @zintrust/core zin new my-app cd my-app zin add db:sqlite zin start That's the basic setup. New projects come with an .env file containing default values: HOST=localhost PORT=7777 LOG_LEVEL=debug So you have some basic configuration in place before you start making changes. What can you build from there? Once your project is running, you can start working with the framework's core features.

articles.body: One of Grand Theft Auto 6 ’s strangest random encounters occurs when you’re offering taxi services, and a man with a beard wearing a dark suit and sunglasses climbs into the backseat with a gun. This can happen if you’re playing as either Jason or Lucia, but both scenes play out the same way: The man wants you to run a red light, ignore phone calls, and drive him to Harborside Park in Vice Beach. He also sounds an awful lot like Tom Cruise, with a calm but forceful demeanor that seems almost sociopathic . articles.title: NASA Awards Contract for NOAA’s Near Earth Orbit Network Program
articles.excerpt: NASA, on behalf of the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), has awarded a contract to Northrop Grumman Systems Corporation for the Sounder for Microwave-Based Applications (SMBA) in…
articles.body: Credit: NASA NASA, on behalf of the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), has awarded a contract to Northrop Grumman Systems Corporation for the Sounder for Microwave-Based Applications (SMBA) instruments on NOAA’s Near Earth Orbit Network (NEON) satellites. The cost-plus-fixed-fee, firm-fixed-price, and time-and-materials hybrid contract has a value of $290.6 million. The period of performance runs from Nov. 23 through April 1, 2042. The work will take place at the awardee’s facility. Under the contract, Northrop Grumman will provide the design, development, production, testing, and mission support for three SMBA instruments, the next generation of low Earth orbit microwave sounders.

articles.title: How sci‑fi imagines sports in microgravity, and how zero‑g sports might actually work
articles.excerpt: How realistic are the zero-g sports we see in sci-fi? We talk to Les Johnson, former Chief Technologist for NASA, to find out.
articles.body: Sports in space have a long and proud tradition, whether it's Alan Shepard playing golf on the moon or the crew of the ISS hosting their own version of the Summer Olympics . The future looks bright as well, with the foundation of the Space Games Federation , the self-described "first governing and sanctioning body for competitive sports played in zero or micro-gravity," co-founded by a NASA astronaut. Not to be outdone, science fiction has expanded the idea of zero-g and low-gravity sports to their logical extent, imagining everything from Doctor Who's zero-g squash to the advanced, gamified combat simulations of Ender's Game.
